error.operatorNeedsExpr: The "{{op}}" operator must be preceded by an expression (position {{pos}}).

thompson.title: Thompson's construction
thompson.detail: Following the expression's structure, a small ε-NFA fragment is built for every subexpression (literal, union, concatenation, star), then these are wired together with ε-transitions. Result: {{count}} states. It can be turned into a DFA with the det(epsfree(·)) chain.

unparseableCell.title: Unparseable cell
unparseableCell.detail: A cell must be either a YAML definition (with a Machine / Grammar key) or an expression (in the form "name = expression").

duplicateDefinition.title: Duplicate definition: "{{name}}"
duplicateDefinition.detail: The name is defined by both cell {{other}} and cell {{index}} — the first definition wins; remove or rename the others.

circularDependency.title: Circular dependency
circularDependency.detail: The definition of "{{name}}" (indirectly) refers to itself: {{chain}}. Break the cycle.

brokenDependency.title: Broken dependency: {{missing}}
brokenDependency.detail: The referenced cell is broken or can't be evaluated yet — fix that one first.

machine.acceptNotInStates: The accepting state ({{state}}) is not among the states

badStoragesField.detail:
For example:
  storages:
    v1: stack
    v2:
      type: queue
      init: A

badInputField.title: The input field ({{input}}) is not the id of a storage
badInputField.detail: Use "head" (the read head), or the name of one of the storages: {{storages}}.

noAcceptSuggestEmptyStorages.title: No accepting state — for acceptance by empty storages, use acceptMode: emptyStorages
noAcceptSuggestEmptyStorages.detail: Without an accepting state and in finalState mode, the machine recognizes the empty language.

invalidTransition.detail: This machine needs {{count}} tokens per line: {{shape}}

noAcceptState.detail: The machine therefore recognizes the empty language.

nondeterministicMachine.title: Nondeterministic machine: more than one transition can match in state {{state}}
nondeterministicMachine.detail: The simulation follows every branch; click a highlighted edge on the graph to pick a specific branch.

fieldHints.init: The start symbol, e.g. init: S

grammar.startNotInNonterminals: The start symbol ({{start}}) is not among the nonterminals

overlappingSymbols.title: Conflicting symbols: {{symbols}}
overlappingSymbols.detail: A symbol cannot be both a terminal and a nonterminal.

invalidRule.title: Invalid rule: "{{line}}"
invalidRule.detail: Form: LEFT -> RIGHT1 | RIGHT2 — e.g. "S -> aA | b". Write $ or ε for the empty word.

grammar.unknownSymbolLeft: Unknown symbol on the left side of the rule: "{{symbol}}"
grammar.ruleDetail: Rule: "{{line}}". Every symbol must be listed in charset or variables.

leftMissingNonterminal.title: The left side of the rule contains no nonterminal: "{{line}}"
leftMissingNonterminal.detail: In a generative grammar, the left side must contain at least one nonterminal.

grammar.unknownSymbolRight: Unknown symbol on the right side of the rule: "{{symbol}}"

rangeTooLarge.title: Range too large in the {{field}} field: "{{range}}"

unknownStorageType.title: Unknown storage type for the "{{id}}" storage
unknownStorageType.detail:
Allowed: stack, queue, tape — with an initial content:
  v1:
    type: stack
    init: Z

badTapeOp.title: Invalid tape operation: "{{tokens}}" ({{storageId}})
badTapeOp.detail: Line: "{{line}}". Form: READ/WRITE MOVE — e.g. "a/b >". Blank symbol: _, "write the same back": &.

badStackOp.title: Invalid storage operation: "{{tokens}}" ({{storageId}})
badStackOp.detail: Line: "{{line}}". Stack form: POP/PUSH — e.g. "Z/AZ"; use $ for ε.

badQueueOp.title: Invalid storage operation: "{{tokens}}" ({{storageId}})
badQueueOp.detail: Line: "{{line}}". Queue form: TAKE/PUT — e.g. "A/BA"; use $ for ε.

needsEpsilonFree.title: The {{op}} operation requires an ε-free automaton
needsEpsilonFree.detail: The automaton contains {{count}} ε-transitions ({{list}}{{ellipsis}}). An ε-transition changes state on reading the empty word, so ε-removal must be done first: for every state we compute its ε-closure, and fold the transitions leaving it back into the original state.

needsDeterministic.title: The {{op}} operation requires a deterministic automaton
needsDeterministic.detail: Nondeterminism found: {{spots}}{{ellipsis}}. In a deterministic automaton, every (state, symbol) pair may have at most one successor state. An equivalent DFA can be built with the powerset construction (determinization).

needsComplete.title: The {{op}} operation requires a complete automaton
needsComplete.detail: Missing transitions: {{spots}}{{ellipsis}} — {{count}} (state, symbol) pairs have no transition defined in total. To complete it, we introduce a new "trap" (rejecting) state and route every missing transition there.

alreadyFree.title: The automaton is already ε-free
alreadyFree.detail: There is no ε-transition, so the operation returns the automaton unchanged.

step1.title: 1. Computing ε-closures
step1.detail: For every state q: E(q) = the set of states reachable from q using only ε-transitions (including q itself).

step2.title: 2. Introducing new transitions
step2.detail: δ'(q, a) = E(δ(E(q), a)) — transitions reachable through the ε-closure are made direct.

step3.title: 3. Extending the accepting states
step3.detailChanged: If E(q) contains an accepting state, q becomes accepting too. New accepting states: {{list}}.
step3.detailUnchanged: No state's ε-closure contains a new accepting state, so the accepting set is unchanged.

alreadyDeterministic.title: The automaton is already deterministic
alreadyDeterministic.detail: Every (state, symbol) pair has at most one transition and there is no ε-transition — the powerset construction only creates the reachable singleton sets.

notComplete.title: The automaton is not complete — the ∅ state may appear
notComplete.detail: Wherever there is no transition, the powerset construction lands in the empty set (∅), which behaves as a trap state. This makes the result a complete DFA.

step.title: Powerset construction
step.detail: Starting from the start state, for every reached state set and every symbol we compute the set of reachable states. Only reachable sets are included. A set is accepting if it contains an original accepting state.

result.title: Result
result.detail: {{count}} states were produced out of the possible 2^{{exponent}} = {{possible}} subsets. Accepting: {{accept}}.

alreadyComplete.title: The automaton is already complete
alreadyComplete.detail: Every (state, symbol) pair has a transition — nothing to do.

nameTaken.title: The state name "{{trap}}" already exists
nameTaken.detail: Completion needs a new, not-yet-used trap-state name.

step.title: Introducing the trap state: {{trap}}
step.detail: The new state {{trap}} is not accepting, and every symbol maps it to itself — once there, it can no longer accept. The missing transitions are routed here.

allReachable.title: Every state is reachable
allReachable.detail: Every state is reachable from the start state — there is nothing to drop.

step.title: Removing unreachable states
step.detail: The states reachable from the start state by a breadth-first traversal remain. Removed: {{removed}}.

unreachableStates.title: Unreachable states
unreachableStates.detail: The state(s) {{states}} are not reachable from the start state — as the first step of minimization we drop them, otherwise spurious equivalence classes could arise.

refine.title: {{round}}. Refinement
refine.detail: A group splits if two of its states lead to different groups on some symbol. New partition: {{partition}}

fixpoint.title: {{round}}. Fixed point
fixpoint.detail: No more splits — the partition is stable: {{partition}}. The groups are the equivalence classes.

alreadyMinimal.title: The automaton was already minimal
alreadyMinimal.detail: Every state ended up in its own equivalence class.

minimized.title: Minimized: {{before}} → {{after}} states
minimized.detail: States grouped into the same class are linguistically indistinguishable: they accept/reject every word the same way.

whyDfa.title: Why is a DFA required?
whyDfa.detail: For an NFA, flipping the accepting states does NOT yield the complement language: an NFA accepts a word if an accepting path EXISTS — after flipping, a rejecting path may still exist and become accepting too.

whyComplete.title: Why is completeness required?
whyComplete.detail: If a transition is missing somewhere, the automaton gets "stuck" and rejects. The complement should accept these words instead — this requires completing the automaton with a trap state first.

step.title: Flipping the accepting states
step.detail: In a complete DFA, every word runs along exactly one path, so swapping accepting/rejecting states yields exactly the complement language. New accepting set: {{accept}}.

hasEpsilon.title: The {{part}} automaton contains an ε-transition
hasEpsilon.detail: The product construction (running both in parallel) expects deterministic, complete automata, because the two automata must step in sync, symbol by symbol. An ε-transition would break this.

nondeterministic.title: The {{part}} automaton is nondeterministic
nondeterministic.detail: The states of the product automaton are (p, q) pairs, with δ((p,q),a) = (δ₁(p,a), δ₂(q,a)) — this requires both δ's to be single-valued.

incomplete.title: The {{part}} automaton is not complete
incomplete.detailUnion: If one automaton gets stuck, the pair can no longer step even though the other could still run — for a union, the other automaton's acceptance still matters. Completion (a trap state) fixes this.
incomplete.detailOther: If one automaton gets stuck, the pair can no longer step even though the other could still run — the result would be incorrect. Completion (a trap state) fixes this.

differentAlphabets.title: The two automata have different alphabets
differentAlphabets.detail: Missing from the first automaton: {{missing1}}. Missing from the second: {{missing2}}. {{mode}} is only meaningful over a common alphabet — extend the alphabets and complete the automata.

acceptRule.union: (p,q) is accepting if p OR q is accepting
acceptRule.intersect: (p,q) is accepting if p AND q are both accepting
acceptRule.difference: (p,q) is accepting if p is accepting but q is NOT (L₁ \ L₂)

step.title: Product construction ({{mode}})
step.detail: The two automata are run in parallel: the states are (p,q) pairs, δ((p,q),a) = (δ₁(p,a), δ₂(q,a)). Acceptance: {{acceptRule}}. Only reachable pairs are built.

info.title: Union built via ε-construction
info.detail: An ε-transition leads from a new start state into both automata's start states. The result is an ε-NFA — it can be determinized with the det(epsfree(·)) chain. (A union of complete DFAs can also be done with the product construction.)

step.title: Union with ε-transitions
step.detail: New start state {{start}}, ε-transitions: {{start}} → {{m1start}}, {{start}} → {{bstart}}. Accepting states: the union of both automata's accepting states.

step.title: Concatenation
step.detail: An ε-transition leads from every accepting state of the first automaton to the second automaton's start state ({{start}}). Accepting: only the second automaton's accepting states. The result is an ε-NFA.

step.title: Kleene closure (star)
step.detail: New start state {{start}} (also accepting — so the empty word is in the language too), an ε-transition to the original start state, and from every accepting state an ε-transition back to {{start}} for repetition.

step.title: Reversal
step.detail: Every transition's direction is reversed, an ε-transition leads from the new start state ({{start}}) to the original accepting states, and the original start state becomes the sole accepting state. L(Mᴿ) = { wᴿ : w ∈ L(M) }.

step.title: Renaming the states
step.detail: States get the names A, B, C… in the order they're visited starting from the start state. The language does not change.

counterexampleSearch.title: Searching for a counterexample in the product automaton
counterexampleSearch.detail: The two automata (made complete and deterministic) are run in parallel, searching for the shortest word accepted by exactly one of them. Found: "{{word}}".

proof.title: Proving equivalence
proof.detail: In every reachable (p,q) state pair of the product automaton, p and q's acceptance status agree, so there is no distinguishing word — the two automata recognize the same language.

classify.leftNotSingleNonterminal: the left side of rule {{rule}} is not a single nonterminal
classify.notRightLinear: the right side of rule {{rule}} is not of the form "terminals + at most one trailing nonterminal"
classify.notLeftLinear: the right side of rule {{rule}} is not of the form "at most one leading nonterminal + terminals"
classify.startEpsilonNotAllowed: S → ε is only allowed if S does not occur on the right side of any rule — but it does here
classify.deletingRule: {{rule}} is a deleting rule (ε is only allowed as S → ε)
classify.epsilonNotOnStart: {{rule}} — ε-rule not on the start symbol
classify.startOnRightWithEpsilon: alongside S → ε, S also occurs on a right side — so the grammar is not in ε-free form

needsRightLinear.title: Only a right-linear (type 3) grammar can be turned into a finite automaton
needsRightLinear.detail: The construction: every nonterminal becomes a state; a rule A → aB becomes the transition A →a B; a rule A → a becomes a transition into a new accepting state; a rule A → ε makes A accepting. See the Chomsky classification panel for the exact reason this grammar doesn't qualify.

step.title: Right-linear grammar → NFA
step.detail: Every nonterminal becomes a state, the start symbol is the start state. From A → aB: an a-transition from A to B; from A → a: a transition to the new ✓ accepting state; for A → ε: A becomes accepting.

tooManyStates.title: Too many states to convert into a grammar
tooManyStates.detail: The automaton has {{count}} states; the single-character nonterminal notation allows at most {{max}} states. Minimization can reduce the number of states.

renamed.title: The states were given nonterminal letters

step.title: NFA → right-linear grammar
step.detail: Every transition q →a p becomes the rule Q → aP, and every accepting state q gives the rule Q → ε. The resulting grammar is type 3 and generates the same language.

needsContextFree.title: Only a context-free (type 2) grammar can be turned into a pushdown automaton
needsContextFree.detail: In the construction, the stack stores the sentential form, so the left side must be a single nonterminal. See the Chomsky classification panel for the exact reason this grammar doesn't qualify.

emptyStackInfo.title: Built a PDA that accepts by empty stack
emptyStackInfo.detail: The stack holds the derivation's current sentential form. If a nonterminal is on top of the stack, a rule is applied (an ε-step); if a terminal, it's matched against the next input letter. A word is accepted exactly when the input is exhausted and the stack is empty.

step.title: CF grammar → PDA (top-down parser)
step.detail: A single state {{q}}. Initial stack content: {{start}}. Rule steps: {{ruleCount}} (ε, A / α), matching steps: {{terminalCount}} (a, a / ε).

needsContextFree.title: ε-removal is defined for context-free grammars
needsContextFree.detail: See the Chomsky classification panel for the exact reason this grammar doesn't qualify.

step1.title: 1. Nullable nonterminals
step1.detailNone: No nullable nonterminal — the grammar is already ε-free.
step1.detailSome: Nullable (derivable to ε): {{nullable}}. A is nullable if A → ε, or A → α and every letter of α is nullable.

step2.title: 2. Extending the rules
step2.detail: For every rule, we build every variant where some subset of its nullable nonterminals is dropped (unless the whole right side would vanish). The ε-rules are then discarded.

step3.title: 3. New start symbol because of ε
step3.detail: The original language contains ε (the start symbol is nullable), so we introduce a new start symbol {{s2}}: {{s2}} → {{start}} | ε. This way the ε-rule remains only on the start symbol.

error.missingCloseParenRegex: Missing closing parenthesis in the regex() call (position {{pos}})
error.missingCommaOrParen: Missing "," or ")" in the function call (position {{pos}})
error.functionNeedsParen: The function name "{{word}}" must be followed by parentheses (position {{pos}})
error.unknownName: Unknown name: "{{word}}" — refer to machines by their name; a letter sequence can only be used inside regex(…) (position {{pos}})

wrongArgCount.exact: The function {{fn}} expects {{n}} argument(s), but {{count}} were given
wrongArgCount.range: The function {{fn}} expects {{n}} or {{alsoOk}} arguments, but {{count}} were given

error.needsFsm: {{ctx}}: expects a finite automaton, but got {{kind}}
error.machineNeedsFsm: {{ctx}}: expects a finite automaton, but {{name}} is {{machineKind}} (storages: {{storages}}). The language recognized by a machine with storage is generally not regular, so there is no automatic conversion — automaton operations only apply to storage-free machines.
error.machineHasStorage: {{name}} cannot be converted to a finite automaton because it has storage ({{storages}}) — only a storage-free machine has an equivalent automaton
error.toFsmExpects: toFsm() expects a grammar, a regular expression, or a storage-free machine
error.parseGeneric: {{message}}. Examples: detM = det(M) · u = union(M1, M2) · r = regex((ab)*+ba) · e = equal(M1, M2)

eval.literalsOnlyInRegex: Letter literals can only be used inside regex(…)

regex.title: Automatically converted the regex {{name}} to an ε-NFA
regex.detail: The operation expects a finite automaton; the regular expression can be converted to an automaton via Thompson's construction — explicitly: toFsm({{name}}).

grammar.title: Automatically converted the grammar {{name}} to a finite automaton
grammar.detail: The operation expects a finite automaton; the right-linear grammar can be converted.
